catalog_quote: 3.2.2 Metrical structure. If we assume that a shift to high vowels {i u} can reflect metrically weak positions in multisyllabic words, we can argue that the second and third of three syllables in a trisyllabic verb with final-syllable rhotic are weak in the bare stem (and related paradigmatic forms), but not in the imperative or some other verb forms. We can see this in alternations like túŋì-rⁿì ‘cause to kneel’ (bare stem) and its imperative túŋɔ́-rⁿɔ̀. For other trisyllabic verb stems (i.e. with a non-rhotic consonant in the final syllable), the second (but not third) syllable is weak even in the imperative, as in kúmúɲù ‘crumple’ (bare stem), imperative kúmúɲɔ́. new_statements.rule_in_words: Togo Kan is described as a tone language (syllable tones H, L and three contours; lexical melodies /H/ and /LH/ with at least one H per stem; extensive grammatical tone overlays). No word-stress or accent is posited: the only metrical remark is that the second (and sometimes third) syllable of trisyllabic verb stems is 'metrically weak', inferred from vowel raising to i/u, i.e. weakness is medial/post-initial, which is compatible with an initial-syllable strong position but Heath does not say so.
new_statements.exceptions: None for stress; the metrical-weakness claim is limited to trisyllabic verb stems (rhotic-final vs other) and varies between bare stem and imperative.
new_statements.domain_note: Word/stem level (verb stems). The word 'stress' occurs only in the 2010/2011 drafts, sec. 13.1 Focalization (2010 p. 249): focus is 'ordinarily not expressed by the form of the focalized constituent itself, except perhaps by a little extra stress' -- phrase-level focal prominence, reworded to 'extra prominence' in the 2015 grammar (p. 275). Secs. 3.8 (pp. 57-58) and 2.1.2 (p. 7) cover intonation (final prolongation, 'dying-quail' pitch decline, clause-final tone-dropping/downdrift).
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog tene1248 [dtk] has no dialect children. Heath 2015 describes the Koporo-Pe dialect of Togo Kan (sec. 1.4.1, p. 5) and treats 'Tene Kan' (Toroli/Azanga area) as the same language (sec. 1.2, p. 1); Prost 1969 described the Pel dialect; Sagara & Andrason 2023 describe 'Teŋukan', the Dourou-community variety, which they call 'one of the dialects of Togo-Teŋukan' (p. 1). All fall under tene1248. The earlier scan's attribution of Heath 2015 to De Gruyter was not verified: the 2015 grammar on record is the Language Description Heritage / University of Michigan online publication (PuRe item_2176494).

sources.note: Tone language (ch. 3.7 Tones, pp. 34-56: syllable tones H, L, <LH>, <HL>, <LHL>; lexical melodies /H/ and /LH/; at least one H per stem). Sec. 3.2.2 'Metrical structure' (p. 13) only argues that the 2nd (and 3rd) syllables of trisyllabic verbs are 'metrically weak' from vowel raising to {i u}. The words 'stress'/'accent' are never used of Togo Kan word prosody; sec. 13.1 (p. 275) says focus is marked at most 'by extra prominence' (phrase level). Sec. 3.8 Intonation contours (pp. 57-58).
